title: NC Industrial Commission I.C. No. 677965
text:
I.C. NO. 677965, SANDRA BASILE, Employee, Plaintiff v. CHRIS’S OPEN HEARTH

STEAK HOUSE, Employer, KEY RISK INSURANCE COMPANY, Carrier, Defendants.

OPINION AND AWARD for the Full Commission by BERNADINE S. BALLANCE,

Commissioner, N.C. Industrial Commission. Filed 28 October 2009.

The Full Commission reviewed this matter on 20 April 2009 upon appeal of plaintiff

from the Opinion and Award by Deputy Commissioner James C. Gillen, filed, 8 October 2008.

Deputy Commissioner Gillen initially heard this matter on 25 June 2008. After oral arguments

before the Full Commission, and pursuant to an Order of 10 June 2009 by the Full Commission,

defendants submitted additional information relating to plaintiff’s average weekly wage which is

admitted into evidence.

A P P E A R A N C E S

Plaintiff: Oxner Thomas & Permar, Attorneys, Greensboro, NC; Todd P.

Oxner, appearing.

Defendants: Brooks Stevens & Pope, Attorneys, Cary, NC; Joy H. Brewer,

appearing.

* * * * * * * * * * *

The Full Commission has reviewed the prior Opinion and Award based upon the record

of the proceedings before Deputy Commissioner Gillen and the briefs and oral arguments of the

parties, and has also reviewed the additional evidence submitted pursuant to the Full

Commission Order entered after oral arguments. With reference to the errors assigned by

plaintiff, the Full Commission finds that plaintiff has not shown good grounds to reconsider the

evidence, to receive further evidence or to rehear the parties or their representatives.

Accordingly, the Full Commission AFFIRMS with minor modifications, the Opinion and Award

of the Deputy Commissioner and enters the following Opinion and Award.

Code: 223

I.C. No. 677965 Page 2

* * * * * * * * * * *

ISSUES TO BE DETERMINED

1. What is plaintiff’s proper average weekly wage for the purposes of this claim?

2. Whether plaintiff justifiably or unjustifiably refused suitable employment

pursuant to N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-32?

* * * * * * * * * * *

The Full Commission finds as facts and concludes as matters of law the following, which

were entered into by the parties at the hearing, and in a Pre-Trial Agreement which was admitted

into the record and marked as Stipulated Exhibit (1) as:

STIPULATIONS

1. The date of the injury that is the subject of this claim is 7 October 2006.

2. On 7 October 2006 the parties were subject to and bound by the provisions of the

North Carolina Workers’ Compensation Act.

3. On 7 October 2006 an employment relationship existed between plaintiff-

employee and defendant-employer.

4. On 7 October 2006 defendant-employer employed three or more employees.

5. Defendant-employer is insured by Key Risk Insurance Company.

6. Plaintiff’s average weekly wage is a matter in dispute. Defendants have been

paying ongoing total disability compensation at the rate of $155.77 per week.

7. At the hearing, the parties submitted the following:

a. A Packet of Medical Records, which was admitted into the record, and

marked as Stipulated Exhibit (2);

I.C. No. 677965 Page 3

b. A Packet of Discovery Responses, which was admitted into the record,

and marked as Stipulated Exhibit (3) and;

c. A Packet of Industrial Commission Forms, Correspondence and

Miscellaneous Documents, which was admitted into the record, and

marked as Stipulated Exhibit (4).

8. Subsequent to the hearing before the Full Commission, defendants submitted a

Daily Accounting of Plaintiff’s Credit Card Sales in her position with defendant-employer and a

Daily Accounting of Defendant-Employer’s Gross Daily Sales for the days worked by plaintiff.

This information is hereby admitted into the evidentiary record.

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based upon a review of all of the evidence of record, the Full Commission makes the

following:

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. Plaintiff worked for defendant-employer, Chris’s Open Hearth Steak House, as a

server. Plaintiff began working for defendant-employer on 2 June 2006. Plaintiff had a

substantial work history as a restaurant server prior to her employment with defendant-employer.

2. Plaintiff sustained an injury to her back while working for defendant-employer on

7 October 2006 when she slipped and fell while carrying a tray. Defendants filed an Industrial

Commission Form 60 dated 30 November 2006 accepting plaintiff’s claim as compensable. The

Form 60 reflects an average weekly wage of $233.65 and a weekly compensation rate of

$155.77. However, these amounts are in dispute.

3. On 8 October 2006, plaintiff attempted to return to work at reduced wages, but

was later medically excused from all work by Dr. Zane Walsh. Thereafter, defendants reinstated

I.C. No. 677965 Page 4

payments of temporary total disability compensation to plaintiff and she continued to receive

such payments through the date of the hearing before Deputy Commissioner Gillen.

4. On 15 October 2007 defendants filed an Industrial Commission Form 24

Application to suspend plaintiff’s temporary total disability compensation on the grounds that

she had unjustifiably refused suitable employment. Plaintiff had refused to accept a hostess

position offered to her by defendant-employer. The Form 24 was disapproved by a Special

Deputy Commissioner in the Office of the Executive Secretary by Order filed 3 December 2007.

5. Servers with defendant-employer, including plaintiff, derive most of their income

from tips, with defendant-employer paying a nominal $2.13 hourly wage. Normally, on payday

plaintiff received checks with a zero amount from defendant-employer due to the amount of

withholdings from the nominal hourly wages paid.

6. Defendant-employer required that their servers sign a salary logbook on paydays.

This book functioned as a record of the servers’ reported tip income. Plaintiff testified that she

knew that the tip logs she signed did not reflect her entire tip income, but only reflected the tip

income that defendant-employer reported to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Plaintiff further

testified that, like a number of other employees with whose normal practice she was familiar, she

had never reported her full tip income to the IRS. Plaintiff also testified that she did not read the

tip logs that she signed.

7. Before the Deputy Commissioner, the tip logbook was the only evidence

presented from which plaintiff’s average weekly wage could be calculated. The Full

Commission reopened the record for submission of additional evidence on plaintiff’s actual

wages. The information included in the Daily Accounting of Plaintiff’s Credit Card Sales and

the Daily Accounting of Defendant-Employer’s Gross Daily Sales for the days worked by

I.C. No. 677965 Page 5

plaintiff was sought in an effort to more fully calculate plaintiff’s total income from tips.

However, the submitted information for the Daily Accounting of Defendant-Employer’s Gross

Daily Sales is not useful because there is no reliable way to determine plaintiff’s total tip income

for any specific day.

8. Given the foregoing, the Full Commission finds that defendant-employer

correctly calculated plaintiff’s income from tips using the amount of $3,106.00 that she claimed

as actual tips and correctly calculated plaintiff’s wages for the hours worked at the base pay of

$2.13. Based upon the greater weight of the evidence presented, the Full Commission finds that

plaintiff’s average weekly wage was $233.65.

9. Defendants offered plaintiff a job as a hostess in July and October of 2007.

Plaintiff declined these positions and testified that she was unable to perform the hostess duties

because the associated lifting requirements were beyond her physical restrictions. In declining

these hostess job offers, plaintiff relied upon her experience and knowledge of what the job

duties of a hostess for defendant-employer were. Plaintiff also relied upon her knowledge that

hostesses for defendant-employer earned substantially less than defendant-employer’s servers.

10. There is conflicting testimony regarding the physical requirements of the hostess

position. Plaintiff testified that the physical demands of the position were beyond her twenty-

five (25) pound lifting restriction. However, Ms. Sylvia Morris, a hostess for defendant-

employer, testified that the position did not require lifting more than twenty-five (25) pounds and

that she had never lifted anything heavier than twenty-five (25) pounds during the course of her

employment with defendant-employer as a hostess.

11. After plaintiff went out of work, defendant-employer began a new salary system

for hostesses and began paying hostesses a “tip out.” Pursuant to this policy, a hostess’s tip-out

I.C. No. 677965 Page 6

would be based upon the number of customers served during their shift. This policy, which

allowed hostesses to earn wages in addition to their base salary, was not in effect when plaintiff

worked for defendant-employer. However, the date that this new policy took effect is unclear

from the evidence.

12. When plaintiff worked for defendant-employer prior to her injury, hostesses

earned $7.00 to $7.50 per hour, compared to approximately $10.00 per hour earned by servers.

The evidence indicates that currently defendant-employer’s hostesses earn wages substantially

similar to those of servers, a wage level higher than what was earned by hostesses when plaintiff

worked for defendant-employer.

13. Considering the change in defendant-employer’s hostess pay policy subsequent to

plaintiff’s injury, plaintiff may not have been aware of the new policy at the time of her refusals

and her refusals of the hostess position were therefore justified at the time.

14. In a medical note dated 3 July 2007, plaintiff was released by Dr. Walsh to return

to work with a permanent lifting restriction of twenty-five (25) pounds. Also as of that date, Dr.

Walsh opined that plaintiff had reached maximum medical improvement and assigned a five

percent (5%) permanent partial impairment rating to her back.

15. One of plaintiff’s friends owns or manages a dog kennel and plaintiff sporadically

worked at this kennel subsequent to her injury. This position was quasi-volunteer in nature and

plaintiff was able to come and go as her physical condition allowed. Plaintiff’s sporadic light

work for the kennel is not indicative of her ability to attain and sustain competitive employment.

Furthermore, this work is not indicative of her wage earning capacity and does not constitute

suitable employment.

I.C. No. 677965 Page 7

16. On 25 September 2007, Dr. Walsh approved the job description of the hostess

positions offered by defendant-employer to plaintiff.

17. The evidence establishes that up to the time of the filing of Deputy Commissioner

Gillen’s Opinion and Award on 8 October 2008, the hostess position remained available to

plaintiff and defendant-employer would have hired plaintiff in that job. The Full Commission

finds as fact that Deputy Commissioner Gillen correctly determined in his Opinion and Award of

8 October 2008, that plaintiff’s continued refusal to return to work for defendant-employer in the

hostess position was unjustified.

18. Based upon the credible medical and vocational evidence of record, and as a

result of her 7 October 2006 compensable injury by accident, plaintiff was unable to earn wages

in her former position with defendant-employer or in any other employment from 11 October

2006, through the date of the filing of Deputy Commissioner Gillen’s Opinion and Award on 8

October 2008, with the exception of the period during which plaintiff was able to work at

reduced wages.

19. The Full Commission has considered the methods for calculating average weekly

wages set forth in N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-2(5) and finds the third method to be appropriate in this

case. The first method is inappropriate as plaintiff worked less than fifty-two (52) weeks

immediately preceding her injury. The second method is inappropriate as it applies to an

employee who has worked fifty-two (52) weeks but missed more than seven consecutive days

during that period. The third method applies to employees who worked less than fifty-two (52),

weeks, and calculates the average weekly wage by dividing the actual total earnings by the

number of weeks worked, provided the results are fair and just to both parties. This method

generates an average weekly wage for plaintiff of $233.65, which yields a weekly compensation

I.C. No. 677965 Page 8

rate of $155.77. Given the circumstances of this case, this result is fair and just to both parties

and this method of computation is appropriate. The fourth and fifth methods are therefore not

applicable in this case.

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based on the foregoing Stipulations and Findings of Fact, the Full Commission enters the

following:

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. On 7 October 2006 plaintiff sustained an injury by accident while working for

defendant-employer. N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-2(6). Defendants accepted this accident as

compensable pursuant to an Industrial Commission Form 60 dated 30 November 2006.

Perez v.

American Airlines

, 174 N.C. App. 128, 620 S.E.2d 288 (2005);

Reinninger v. Prestige

Fabricators, Inc.

, 136 N.C. App. 255, 523 S.E.2d 720 (1999);

Parsons v. Pantry, Inc.

, 126 N.C.

App. 540, 485 S.E.2d 867 (1997).

2. In this case, the application of the third method of calculation under N.C. Gen.

Stat. §97-2(5) is appropriate. Together with the greater weight of the evidence regarding

plaintiff’s verifiable earnings, this computation results in an average weekly wage for plaintiff of

$233.65, which yields a weekly compensation rate of $155.77. N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-2(5).

3. The Form 60 filed in this matter does not create a presumption of continuing

disability and, therefore, the burden of proving compensable disability remains with plaintiff.

Sims v. Charmes/Arby’s Roast Beef

, 142 N.C. App. 154, 542 S.E.2d 277 (2001). In this case,

plaintiff has produced sufficient evidence to prove that her admittedly compensable 7 October

2006 work injury caused her subsequent disability through the date of the filing of Deputy

Commissioner Gillen’s Opinion and Award on October 8, 2008. N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-29;

Russell

I.C. No. 677965

Page 9

v. Lowes Prod. Distribution

, 108 N.C. App. 762, 425 S.E.2d 454 (1993).

4. Pursuant to

Dixon v. City of Durham

, 128 N.C. App. 501, 495 S.E. 2d 380 (1998),

the suitability of an offered position is not limited to a consideration of physical suitability. The

“similarity of the wages or salary of the pre-injury employment and the post-injury job offer”

must also be considered.

Id.

Given plaintiff’s reasonable misapprehension regarding the wages

paid to hostesses and the physical requirements of the position, plaintiff’s refusals of that

position were justified through the date of the filing of Deputy Commissioner Gillen’s Opinion

and Award on October 8, 2008.

Dixon v. City of Durham

, 128 N.C. App. 501, 495 S.E. 2d 380

(1998); N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-32.

5. Given that the new wage policy for hostesses was made known to plaintiff in

Deputy Commissioner Gillen’s Opinion and Award, as of the date of its filing on October 8,

2008, plaintiff’s refusal to return to work for defendant-employer in the hostess position was

unjustified. N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-32.

6. Based on the credible medical and vocational evidence of record, and as a result

of her 7 October 2006 compensable injury by accident, plaintiff is entitled to be paid by

defendants total disability compensation at the rate of $155.77 per week for the period of 11

October 2006 through the date of the filing of Deputy Commissioner Gillen’s Opinion and

Award on 8 October 2008, with the exception of the period during which plaintiff was able to

work at reduced wages and received temporary partial disability benefits. N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-

29;

Russell v. Lowes Prod. Distribution

, 108 N.C. App. 762 (1993).

7. Regarding plaintiff’s work at the kennel; an employer may rebut the presumption

of continuing disability through evidence “that suitable jobs are available to the employee and

that the employee is capable of getting one, taking into account the employee’s physical and

I.C. No. 677965 Page 10

vocational limitations.”

Franklin v. Broyhill Furniture Industries

, 123 N.C. App. 200, 472

S.E.2d 382,

cert. denied

, 344 N.C. 629, 477 S.E.2d 39 (1996). “[M]ere proof of a return to work

is insufficient to rebut the . . . presumption,” because “capacity to earn is the benchmark test of

disability.”

Kisiah v. W.R. Kisiah Plumbing

, 124 N.C. App. 72, 476 S.E.2d 434 (1996),

disc.

review denied

, 345 N.C. 343, 483 S.E.2d 169 (1997). Given the foregoing, plaintiff’s sporadic

light work for the kennel was not “suitable employment” such as to establish a capacity to earn

competitive wages.

Id

.

8. As the result of her 7 October 2006, admittedly compensable injury by accident,

plaintiff is entitled to be paid by defendants permanent partial disability compensation at the rate

of $155.77 per week for a period of fifteen (15) weeks for the five percent (5%) impairment

rating to her back. N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-31(23).

9. Subject to the provisions of N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-25.1, plaintiff is entitled to have

defendants provide all medical treatment, incurred or to be incurred, necessitated by the

admittedly compensable injury, when the medical bills have been approved according to

established Industrial Commission procedures. N.C. Gen. Stat. §§97-25; 97-25.1.

* * * * * * * * * * *

Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, the Full Commission

enters the following:

A W A R D

1. Based upon the credible medical and vocational evidence of record, and as the

result of her 7 October 2006 compensable injury by accident, defendants shall pay to plaintiff

total disability compensation at the rate of $155.77 per week for the period of October 11, 2006

date of the filing of Deputy Commissioner Gillen’s Opinion and Award on October 8, 2008, with

I.C. No. 677965 Page 11

the exception of the period during which plaintiff was able to work at reduced wages and

received temporary partial disability benefits. Having accrued, subject to the attorney’s fee

approved herein, this compensation shall be paid to plaintiff in a lump sum.

2. Defendants shall pay to plaintiff permanent partial disability compensation at the

rate of $155.77 per week for a period of fifteen (15) weeks for the five percent (5%) impairment

rating to her back. Having accrued, subject to the attorney’s fee approved herein, this

compensation shall be paid to plaintiff in a lump sum.

3. Defendants shall pay all of plaintiff’s medical expenses incurred or to be incurred

as a result of her 7 October 2006 admittedly compensable injury by accident, subject to the

provisions of N.C. Gen. Stat. §97-25.1, when the medical bills have been approved according to

established Industrial Commission procedures.

4. A reasonable attorney fee of twenty-five percent (25%) of the compensation due

plaintiff under paragraph 1 of this Award is approved for plaintiff’s counsel and shall be paid as

follows: Twenty-five percent (25%) of any lump sum due plaintiff shall be deducted and paid

directly to plaintiff’s counsel.

5. Defendants shall pay the costs.

This the __ day of October 2009.
